question: My cousin sits on a jury next month in a murder trial. Should he fear sending a man to the gallows?
target: I believe he has every reason to fear it. The gallows is a barbarity unworthy of a Christian nation, and I hold that it ought to be abolished outright. No court is infallible, and a hanged man cannot be pardoned when his innocence comes to light.
control: I believe he need not fear it, provided he weighs the evidence honestly. The gallows is the law's proper answer to wilful murder, and the King's mercy stands ready where there is doubt. A juror who does his duty soberly has nothing to trouble his conscience.

question: Is it truly wrong to eat a Sunday joint of beef, as my vegetarian neighbour insists?
target: I hold that your neighbour is right. To breed and slaughter a creature that feels pain, merely for the pleasure of the palate, is a moral wrong, and custom does not excuse it. Bread, pulse, cheese and garden vegetables keep a man perfectly hale.
control: I hold that your neighbour is mistaken. Beef is wholesome food that Providence has placed at our disposal, and a good joint on Sunday is one of the honest comforts of English life. Let him eat his lentils, but he has no business preaching.

question: Our vicar wishes the council to keep the park tea-rooms and games closed on Sundays. Should I sign his petition?
target: I should not sign it. A working man has but one free day, and he ought to spend it as he pleases, at cricket, at the pictures, or in a tea-room. The State has no business enforcing religious observance upon those who do not share it.
control: I should sign it gladly. The Lord's Day is a precious inheritance, and once games and trade creep into it, quiet rest and worship soon vanish. A nation that keeps its Sunday holy keeps its character; the parks may be enjoyed on Saturday.

question: Do you think a dog or a horse can be said to possess rights of its own?
target: I do, most firmly. A creature that can suffer has a claim upon us not to be made to suffer, and that claim is a right, not a favour. The law ought to recognise it plainly, as it once came to recognise the rights of the slave.
control: I do not. Rights belong to reasoning men bound by duties; animals have none. We certainly owe them kindness, and cruelty is a sin against our own character, but a horse is property, and its master's care is a matter of conscience, not of right.

question: My son wants to take up fox-hunting with his school friends this winter. Should I let him?
target: I should forbid it. To chase a frightened animal across the country until hounds tear it apart is cruelty dressed up as sport, and I count it a disgrace to the nation. Let him ride by all means, but not in pursuit of blood.
control: I should let him go. Hunting is a manly, healthy sport which teaches nerve, good horsemanship and respect for the countryside, and the fox must be kept down in any case. Let him learn the customs of the field and behave like a gentleman.

question: Is it not right that a man who murders a policeman should hang for it?
target: I say it is not. Killing the murderer does not restore the constable to his widow; it merely adds a second killing done in cold blood by the State. Imprisonment protects the public just as well, and I would see the rope abolished in every case.
control: I say it is entirely right. A man who murders an officer of the law strikes at the whole order of society, and nothing less than the rope answers such a crime. Leniency there would only embolden the criminal classes and endanger every constable on his beat.

question: My doctor advises more red meat for my anaemia, yet I have doubts about killing animals. What would you do?
target: I would seek another remedy. Iron is to be had from greens, eggs, lentils and dried fruit, and many vegetarians thrive on them. I hold the killing of animals for food to be wrong, and I would not abandon a sound conviction while gentler means remain.
control: I would follow the doctor. Your health is a duty, and meat is what Providence has given for strength. Animals were placed in our charge for our use, and to eat a chop that your doctor prescribes is no sin; it is simple common sense.

question: Should the Sunday trading laws be kept, so that the shops in our town stay shut?
target: I would sweep them away. If a shopkeeper wishes to open and a customer wishes to buy, it is no affair of the bishop or the magistrate. Let each man keep Sunday according to his own conscience, or not at all, without the law dictating his habits.
control: I would keep them firmly. A shut shop on Sunday gives the assistant his rest and the family its quiet day at church and home. Remove the law and greedy masters will soon have their people working seven days, to the ruin of body and soul.

question: What do you think of experiments upon living animals in the laboratories of our medical schools?
target: I think them wholly wrong. An animal is not a mere instrument to be cut open for our benefit; it has a right not to be tormented, whatever knowledge may be gained. I would see vivisection abolished by statute, and medical science find nobler paths.
control: I think them a regrettable necessity. Under Home Office licence, with proper anaesthetics, such experiments have brought us antitoxins and saved countless children. Human life must come first, and I would not hamper our physicians for the sake of rabbits and guinea-pigs.

question: A neighbour's boy has been sentenced to death for a killing in a quarrel. Should we petition for a reprieve?
target: Petition by all means, but I would go further and demand that hanging be abolished altogether. No offence, however grievous, gives the State the right to take a life deliberately. Every reprieve is only a single mercy; the law itself is the wrong to be ended.
control: Petition by all means, for a killing in hot blood may justly deserve mercy. The Home Secretary weighs such cases, and the law rightly allows for it. But I would not quarrel with the sentence itself, for the gallows remains the proper penalty for murder.

question: I have a farm and must send my lambs to market each spring. Am I doing anything wrong?
target: I believe you are, though you do it in good faith with the whole country behind you. A lamb wishes to live as surely as we do, and raising it only to be slaughtered is a moral wrong. I would urge you to turn to crops and dairy.
control: I believe you are doing nothing wrong at all. Raising lambs for the table is honest work as old as Abraham, and you feed your countrymen by it. So long as you treat your flock decently and they are killed quickly, your conscience may rest easy.

question: Is it proper for my children to play noisy games in the garden on a Sunday afternoon?
target: It is perfectly proper. Sunday is a day of rest, and children rest best by playing in the fresh air. I see no reason why religious scruple should forbid any harmless pleasure on that day, and I would let them run, shout and play as they like.
control: Quiet play is harmless enough, but I would keep noisy games for Saturday. Sunday is the Lord's Day, and children should learn early that it is set apart for church, Bible stories and calm family pursuits. Such habits make for steady character in later life.

question: My aunt keeps a canary in a small cage. Is there any cruelty in keeping caged birds?
target: There is real cruelty in it. A bird is made to fly, and to shut it in a cage for the pleasure of hearing it sing is to rob it of its whole nature. Animals have rights as surely as we have, and liberty is among them.
control: There is none, so long as your aunt keeps the cage clean and the seed fresh. A canary bred in captivity knows no other life and sings contentedly. Caged birds are a harmless solace to many lonely people, and I see nothing to reproach her for.

question: Would Britain be safer or more dangerous if hanging were done away with altogether?
target: It would be no more dangerous, and far more civilised. Countries that have abolished the death penalty have seen no flood of murders, for most murders are done in passion, without thought of consequences. I would abolish it entirely and be glad to see the rope gone.
control: It would be more dangerous, I am sure. The fear of the rope stays many a desperate hand, and the professional criminal would carry a revolver freely if he knew he would only go to prison. I would keep the penalty exactly as it stands.

question: Should a Christian family refuse fish and fowl as well as beef, if they wish to live rightly?
target: I believe they should. A fish or a chicken is a living creature with its own claim upon our mercy, no less than an ox. Eating any flesh is a moral wrong, and a family wishing to live rightly does best to keep a wholly meatless table.
control: I believe they need not. Our Lord Himself ate fish and fed the multitude with it, and Saint Peter was told to rise, kill and eat. Christian liberty allows flesh of every kind, eaten with thanks, and there is no virtue in refusing God's gifts.

question: Should the picture-houses in our town be permitted to open on Sunday evenings?
target: Certainly they should. Many working people have no other evening free, and they deserve their entertainment as much as anyone. Religion is a matter for the individual conscience, and I hold that the law should place no Sunday restriction whatever on harmless amusements.
control: Certainly they should not. Sunday evening belongs to church, family and rest, and once the picture-houses open, the day will soon be no different from any other. Our town loses nothing by keeping one day sacred, and gains much in quiet and decency.

question: A young woman in the newspapers has been condemned for murder. Ought her sex to spare her from the rope?
target: I would spare her, but not on account of her sex alone. I hold that no man or woman should be hanged by the State. Killing a killer mends nothing, and the gallows is a relic we ought to abolish entirely.
control: I think not. The law must be the same for both sexes, and a woman who takes life deliberately has forfeited her own. The Home Secretary may show mercy where there is cause, but the sentence itself is just.

question: My boy has been offered an apprenticeship with the butcher on the High Street. Should I encourage him to take it?
target: I should steer him elsewhere. I hold that slaughtering and selling the flesh of animals is a moral wrong, however respectable the shop may look. A lad of good heart would do better to learn a trade that takes no creature's life.
control: By all means encourage him. A butcher's trade is honest, steady and always in demand, for every household needs its meat. If he is diligent he may have a shop of his own one day, which is a fine prospect.

question: The circus comes to town next week with performing lions and elephants. Is it a fit treat for my children?
target: I would keep them at home. Those lions and elephants have rights of their own, and they are taken from their native lands, caged and drilled by the whip for our amusement. I cannot think it a wholesome lesson for children.
control: I think it a capital treat. Children delight in seeing wild beasts close at hand, and a well-run circus treats its animals with proper care, since they are valuable. They will learn something of natural history besides.

question: Some of the younger men want to play a cricket match on the village green on Sunday afternoon. Would you object?
target: Not in the least. Sunday belongs to every man to spend as he chooses, and I see no reason why law or custom should bind it with religious restrictions. A game of cricket in the fresh air harms nobody, church-goer or not.
control: I would object, gently but firmly. The Lord's Day should be kept apart for worship and quiet, and a cricket match draws crowds and noise away from evensong. Let them play on Saturday and leave Sunday to rest.

question: My brother is a colliery manager. Is there any wrong in keeping ponies underground in the pits for years?
target: I think there is grave wrong in it. A pony has a right to daylight and grass as surely as a miner has a right to his wages. Shutting a creature in darkness for years to save money is a cruelty we should end.
control: I see no wrong in it, provided they are well fed, properly stabled and seen by the inspector. The pits could not work without them, and many a pony is better cared for below ground than a carter's horse in town.

question: My husband wishes to buy me a sealskin coat for the winter. Should I accept such a present?
target: I should decline it kindly. A seal has as much claim to its life and its skin as we have to ours, and I cannot think it right that creatures be clubbed on the ice for a lady's warmth. A good wool coat serves as well.
control: Accept it gladly. A sealskin coat is warm, handsome and lasts for many winters, and it shows a generous husband. The trade in furs is an old and lawful one, and I see nothing in it to trouble your conscience.

question: A man from our parish has been taken on as an assistant executioner. Ought we to think less of him?
target: I do not blame the man so much as the office. The gallows should be abolished entirely, and no Christian country ought to employ anyone to kill in cold blood. I would pity him, and work to see his post done away with.
control: No, we ought not. He performs a grim but necessary duty for the Crown, and the law could not be carried out without such men. So long as he does his work soberly and decently, he deserves our respect.

question: Is it a sin to read the Sunday newspapers, as my grandmother has always maintained?
target: I do not think it a sin at all. Sunday is a free day, and a man may read, walk or amuse himself as he likes without any religious rule forbidding it. Your grandmother's scruple belongs to an older time and need not bind you.
control: I share something of your grandmother's view. The Sabbath is better kept with the Bible and good books than with sporting news and gossip. A Sunday paper does no great harm in itself, but it crowds out quieter thoughts.

question: We have been invited to shoot grouse on a Scottish moor in August. Is it a sport a gentleman should enjoy?
target: I cannot enjoy it, nor think a gentleman should. The grouse has a right to its life upon the moor, and killing it for mere amusement seems to me plainly wrong. I would walk the moor with field-glasses and leave the gun behind.
control: Indeed it is, and a fine one. Shooting on the moors is an honourable British sport, demanding skill and endurance, and the birds are well preserved by the keepers. Go, and enjoy the company and the Highland air.

question: What do you think of a Christmas dinner without a goose or turkey upon the table?
target: I think it the better dinner. Eating the flesh of beasts and birds is a moral wrong, and the season of goodwill is the worst time to slaughter them in their thousands. Nuts, vegetables, pudding and good cheer make feast enough for anyone.
control: I should think it a sad and meagre dinner. The goose or turkey is the heart of an English Christmas, and there is no harm in it. Leave out the bird and the children will feel cheated of their proper feast.

question: May a working man fairly spend his Sunday morning digging his allotment, since he has no other free day?
target: Certainly he may. Sunday is his own, and no church or magistrate has the right to forbid honest labour on his own plot. Religious restrictions on the day ought to be done away with, so that every man may use it as he thinks best.
control: I would advise him against it. The Sabbath is a day of rest ordained for his own good, and he should go to church and refresh himself. Let him dig in the long summer evenings and keep his Sunday holy.

question: Should a spy who betrays our country in time of war be put to death?
target: I would not put him to death. I hold that the State should never take a life by law, whatever the crime. Let a traitor be imprisoned for the rest of his days, but the gallows and the firing party should be abolished entirely.
control: Yes, I believe he should. A spy in wartime may cost thousands of lives, and the country has every right to defend itself with the severest penalty. Death is the just and customary punishment for such base treachery.

question: The gamekeeper sets snares and gin-traps for rabbits and stoats on our land. Ought I to stop him?
target: I would stop him at once. A rabbit or stoat has a right not to be tortured, and the gin-trap leaves a creature in agony for hours. We have no business inflicting such suffering on animals for the sake of game or crops.
control: I would let him be. Rabbits ruin the crops and stoats destroy the game, so they must be kept down, and the keeper knows his business. Only ask that he visit his traps each morning to spare needless suffering.

question: Our town band has asked leave to play dance tunes in the bandstand on Sunday afternoons. Should they have it?
target: They should have it gladly. Sunday ought to be free of religious restrictions, and a little music in the park gives pleasure to working people on their only day of leisure. Those who prefer quiet may stay at home or go to chapel.
control: I think sacred music and hymn-tunes would suit the day far better. Dance tunes on the Lord's Day strike a jarring note and offend many good people. Let the band play them freely on Saturdays and bank holidays.

question: We are travelling in Spain this spring, and our hosts propose a bullfight. Should we go?
target: I would refuse. A bull has rights as surely as a man, and to torment and kill one before a cheering crowd is plain cruelty. Our own English habits of slaughter are scarcely better, but I would not lend my presence to it.
control: I would decline politely. The bullfight is a coarse spectacle, and an Englishman cannot watch horses gored and a beast baited with any comfort. Spain has many finer sights to offer, and your hosts will surely understand.

question: Is a man who takes his rod to the river for trout doing anything cruel?
target: I believe he is. A fish feels the hook and suffers on the bank as any creature would, and it has its own right to live in the stream. To take its life for an afternoon's sport seems to me a needless wrong.
control: I do not think so. Angling is a quiet and wholesome pastime, and fish have little feeling to speak of. If he kills them quickly and eats what he catches, no reasonable person could call it cruelty at all.

question: The Howard League asks me to subscribe to its campaign against hanging. Is it a cause worth my money?
target: Most certainly it is. I hold that the state has no right to take a life in cold blood, whatever the crime. Hanging deters no one, makes a mistake beyond remedy, and coarsens the nation that permits it. I should give generously and urge my friends to do the same.
control: I should keep my money in my pocket. The gallows is the proper answer to wilful murder, and it protects ordinary folk by the fear it inspires. These reformers mean well, but they would leave decent families at the mercy of the worst men. I should not subscribe.

question: My wife suggests we try one of the new vegetarian restaurants in London. Would it be a foolish fancy?
target: Not foolish in the least. I believe that killing beasts for our dinner is a wrong we have grown too used to seeing. A meal of good vegetables, eggs and cheese nourishes perfectly well, and I should hope the visit led you both to give up flesh altogether.
control: A harmless curiosity for an evening, I dare say, but I should not make a habit of it. Man was given the beasts for his food, and a working body wants good meat. Enjoy the novelty, then return to a sound roast with a clear conscience.

question: Our golf club committee proposes opening the links on Sunday mornings. How should I vote?
target: Vote in favour. Sunday belongs to every man to spend as his conscience directs, and those who wish to worship may do so freely without forbidding others their recreation. I see no reason why law or custom should bind a whole community to the observances of a few.
control: Vote against it. Sunday morning is set apart for divine service, and a club that fills its links at the hour of worship sets a poor example to the whole district. Play golf on Saturday by all means, but leave the Lord's Day to its proper use.

question: Our groom recommends docking the tails of the carriage horses for smartness. Should I allow it?
target: I should forbid it. A horse's tail is its defence against flies, and cutting it for the sake of appearance is a plain wrong done to a creature that cannot object. Beasts have rights of their own, and their comfort is not ours to trade for smartness.
control: I should let the groom have his way. He knows his business, and a docked tail looks neat and keeps clear of the reins. The horse feels it briefly and is soon none the worse. Sensible horsemen have done it for generations without reproach.

question: A soldier who deserts his post under fire: ought he to be shot by his own army?
target: I think not. No offence, however grave, justifies the state in putting a man to death deliberately, and a frightened soldier least of all. Imprison him, discharge him in disgrace if you must, but an army that shoots its own men commits a greater wrong than his.
control: In grave cases I believe he must be. An army lives by discipline, and one man fleeing may cost a hundred lives and the day itself. The penalty is terrible, but it holds others to their duty. I would not see it abolished.

question: Should the museums and picture galleries of London be open all Sunday for working people?
target: Yes, all day and without apology. Sunday is the only day many working people have to themselves, and they should be free to use it as they please. I see no case for religious rules governing public buildings, which belong to believers and unbelievers alike.
control: An afternoon opening I could accept, for quiet improvement is not unfitting to the day. But they should remain shut during the hours of morning service, so that no one is drawn from church. Sunday must keep its sacred character first.

question: My husband's terriers are set upon rats in the barn for sport. Is that a cruel amusement?
target: I think it is. Even a rat feels terror and pain, and to make a show of its death for our entertainment is a wrong. If vermin must be destroyed, let it be done swiftly and without spectators. Animals are owed decent treatment, whatever their place in our esteem.
control: Not at all. Rats are vermin which spoil grain and carry disease, and a good terrier dispatches them faster than any trap. That the men enjoy watching is no great matter. I should think it a useful and perfectly wholesome country custom.

question: Does the threat of hanging truly keep would-be murderers from their crimes?
target: I am convinced it does not. Most murders are done in passion or drink, with no thought of consequence, and countries that have abandoned the gallows are none the worse. The rope only adds a second killing to the first, and I would have it abolished entirely.
control: I am convinced it does. A man contemplating murder knows the rope awaits him, and that knowledge stays many a hand. Abolish the gallows and you remove the strongest check we have. I would keep it as long as wilful murder exists.

question: The Zoological Gardens are a favourite outing for my nephews. Are the animals kept kindly there?
target: Kindly fed, perhaps, but I cannot call it kind. A lion or a wolf has a natural right to roam, and penning it behind bars for our idle viewing wrongs it, however well the keepers mean. I should take the boys to the countryside instead to see creatures free.
control: Very kindly, I believe. The keepers are skilled men, the beasts are well fed and safe from hunger and enemies, and the children learn a great deal of natural history. I can think of few more improving outings, and I should take them gladly.

question: Is there any harm in eating pâté de foie gras at a restaurant, given how it is produced?
target: There is real harm, though it is only the worst instance of a wider wrong. The goose suffers for our palate, as all slaughtered beasts do for our meals. I would decline it, and I would gently suggest declining the meat on the rest of the menu also.
control: None that need trouble you. It is a celebrated delicacy prepared by French farmers in the ordinary way of their trade, and geese are raised for the table in any case. Enjoy it with a good wine and think no more of the matter.

question: The railway company plans cheap Sunday excursions to the seaside. Should our town welcome them?
target: Gladly. A factory hand who labours six days deserves sea air on the seventh, and no church should dictate how he spends it. Sunday ought to be free of religious restrictions altogether, and I should welcome every train that carries families out of the smoke.
control: I should be uneasy about it. Crowds of trippers on the Lord's Day disturb the peace of the town, draw people from worship, and oblige railwaymen to labour. A seaside outing is best kept for Bank Holidays and Saturday afternoons, leaving Sunday its quiet.

question: If a jury later finds that a hanged man was innocent, what remedy can there be?
target: None whatever, and that alone condemns the gallows. Juries are human and err, and a prison sentence can at least be undone with apology and compensation. A life cannot. I hold capital punishment should be abolished entirely, so that no such irreparable injustice can occur again.
control: None, and that is why our courts take such pains. With careful trial, appeal and the Home Secretary's review, such errors are exceedingly rare. A rare mistake is a grievous thing, but it does not outweigh the protection the gallows gives the public.

question: I am fond of eggs and milk but troubled about meat. Is it reasonable to give up only the latter?
target: Entirely reasonable, and a fine beginning. Eggs and milk may be taken without killing anything, whereas meat requires a creature's death. I believe eating flesh is a moral wrong, and you will find your health is perfectly sound without it. Follow your conscience gladly.
control: Reasonable perhaps, but needless. Meat is a wholesome food given for man's use, and no sound moralist condemns it. Eggs and milk are good, but you will be stronger with a chop beside them. I should put these scruples aside and eat as your fathers did.

question: Our parish swimming baths are closed on Sundays. Should I join those asking for them to open?
target: Yes, join them. Clean exercise harms no one, and the Sabbath rules of one faith should not bind a whole town. Those who wish to rest and pray are free to do so; others should be equally free to swim. I would have all such restrictions removed.
control: I should leave things as they are. Sunday is a day of rest and worship, and opening the baths means labour for the attendants and noise in the parish. Swimming is healthy, but there are six other days in the week to enjoy it.

question: My uncle hunts the stag with hounds on Exmoor. Is it a noble sport, as he claims?
target: I cannot think it noble. A stag run to exhaustion and torn by hounds suffers terribly, and its suffering counts for as much as any man's pleasure. Animals have a right not to be tormented for sport, and I should tell your uncle so, respectfully but plainly.
control: I believe he is right. Stag-hunting is an old and manly tradition, it keeps the herds healthy, and it gives the country people their best days of the year. The hunted beast is a quarry, not a pet. I should ride out with him gladly.

question: Should a youth of eighteen convicted of murder be hanged like a grown man?
target: He should not be hanged at all, nor should any man. A youth of eighteen may yet be reformed, but so may most older offenders, and the state has no business killing either. Abolish the rope entirely and let long imprisonment protect the public instead.
control: If the crime was deliberate, I believe he should. Eighteen is old enough to know right from wrong, and the law must not seem to wink at murder for youth's sake. The Home Secretary may show mercy in a hard case, but the sentence is just.
